replies.author: @abcd-ab77
replies.text: True, those entities existed pre-Ottoman. However, when the Empire collapsed, borders weren't drawn neatly based on ancient history; they were shaped by the geopolitical interests of global powers (Russia, Austria, etc.) and aggressive nationalism. In fact, under centuries of Ottoman rule (Pax Ottomana), the peoples of the region had lived in a much more peaceful, stable, and secure environment while preserving their own faiths and cultures. Therefore, it wasn't a simple 'get the piece of cake back' situation, but a chaotic process that led to massive tragedies. Furthermore, modern Greece was not a result of historical continuity, but was established as a geopolitical 'project state' engineered by great powers (Britain, France, and Russia) to dismantle the Ottoman Empire. In fact, they didn't even choose a local leader; instead, an Austrian/German monarch (King Otto of Bavaria) was appointed to rule this newly fabricated state. Also, to make a historical correction: there was never a homogeneous Greek state called "Byzantium". Scientifically, the term "Byzantine" was coined much later in the 16th century by the German historian Hieronymus Wolf. The empire's actual name was the Eastern Roman Empire, and its citizens (including Greeks) identified themselves as "Romans" (Romaioi), not Greeks. Therefore, modern nationalistic claims in the Balkans are mostly 19th-century constructs rather than a direct continuation of ancient states.

replies.text:
​@kingtryfon5702 True, there were major historical Greek city-states along the coasts of Ionia and Pontus during antiquity, but you are experiencing a significant conceptual confusion here. Modern Greece is the legal or political continuation of neither the scattered city-states of the ancient era nor the Roman/Byzantine Empire. The Eastern Roman Empire was never a Greek nation-state; they always identified themselves as 'Romans' (Romaioi). The centralized and modern State of Greece we know today is a very recent state, established for the first time in history in 1830 through the London Protocol after breaking away from the Ottoman Empire.
Therefore, you cannot equate the example of Pomerania or Silesia—which were modern German territories for centuries where Germans lived continuously until 1945—with Greece's ancient colonial/city maps from thousands of years ago. Trying to claim rights over today's nation-state borders based on ancient civilization heritages is just as absurd as Italians opening a map of the Roman Empire and declaring the entire Mediterranean basin as their own territory.
